## Initial testing of Alfvén eigenmode feedback control with machine-learning observers on DIII-D

Andrew Rothstein1, Azarakhsh Jalalvand1, Joseph Abbate1, Keith Erickson2

and Egemen Kolemen1,2,∗

1 Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, United States of America 2 Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, Princeton, NJ, United States of America

E-mail: ekolemen@pppl.gov

Received 8 February 2024, revised 20 June 2024 Accepted for publication 18 July 2024 Published 31 July 2024

Abstract A first of its kind fully data-driven system has been developed and implemented into the DIII-D plasma control system to detect and control Alfvén eigenmodes (AE) in real-time. Susceptibility to fast ion-induced AE is a challenge in fully non-inductive tokamak operation, which significantly reduces fast-particle confinement and results in degraded fusion gain. Controlling AEs in real-time to improve fast-ion confinement is, hence, important for future advanced tokamak fusion reactors. The models were implemented and tested in experiments which showed that neural networks (NN) are highly effective in detecting 5 types of AE (BAE, EAE, LFM, RSAE, TAE) using high resolution ECE. To estimate the neutron deficit, a NN has been trained that outputs the classical neutron rate using similar inputs to NUBEAM. Also a preliminary ML-based proportional control has been designed and gone through initial testing in experiment to use feedback-control on the neutral beam power to achieve desired amplitude of AE modes and neutron deficits. The effect of AEs on fast-ion confinement is measured by analysing the gap in classical neutron rate from the proposed NN-based NUBEAM and the measured neutron rate.

Keywords: Alfvén eigenmodes, machine learning, DIII-D, control, neural networks

(Some figures may appear in colour only in the online journal)

## 1. Introduction

Controlled management of super-thermal particle populations is essential for optimizing the design of planned fusion systems like ITER. Fusion reactions generate useful energetic particle distributions that are critical for sustaining fusion via

alpha self-heating in an ignited burning plasma. Energetic particles produced by external heating methods like neutral beam injectors (NBI) or ion cyclotron resonance heating can raise plasma temperatures to fusion-relevant levels, but they also hold the potential to destabilize magnetohydrodynamic fluctuations. Unconstrained energetic ions have the capacity to carry away fusion power, degrade plasma performance, and damage plasma facing components [1]. Given the threat arising from Alfvénic perturbations, the control of Alfvén eigenmodes (AE) is a critical research domain. AE occurrences are detected routinely during experimental NBI campaigns [2, 3] and are expected within ITER [4– 8]. Detecting and regulating AEs within high-performance

plasmas capable of sustaining ignition, while mitigating damage from unconfined particles, remains a paramount objective for ITER [9, 10]. Many actuators exist to control AEs and many have been tried with various levels of success such as localized electron cylcotron resonant heating, electron cyclotron current drive, and externally applied resonant magnetic perturbations [11]. Of particular interest is the modulation of NBIs because of the highly anisotropic nature of the energetic particle distributions created by NBI heating. Work has been done to tailor the energetic particle distribution by modifying NBI power to reduce AE activity [12–15]. Data-driven methods provides an alternative path towards AE control since they can augment control techniques in real time with fast response times and require less inputs. A suite of fluctuation diagnostics such as electron cyclotron emission (ECE), CO2 interferometry, beam emission spectroscopy and magnetics can be used to reliably detect AEs on DIII-D [16]. More recently, work has been done to make real-time detection of AEs using ECE [3, 17] and the CO2 interferometer [18]. Although ECE measurements are high resolution and can measure AE fluctuations with good signalto-noise, issues associated with resonances and cutoff frequencies poses challenges for AE detection. To cover some of the limitations of an ECE-based AE predictor, in this work we investigate the training of neural networks (NN) for detecting AEs using ECE as well as a secondary method of neutron deficit. When AEs are present, the measured neutron rate can be up to 40% lower than the classically expected neutron rate and it is especially correlated with Toroidal AEs (TAEs) [19–21]. Here the classical neutron rate is defined as the neutron rate that would occur if there was no transport by instabilities. This relationship was later shown to be causal [22], providing the opportunity to infer the presence of AEs by comparing classically expected neutron rates to measured neutron rates. The NUBEAM code [23] as a part of the larger TRANSP suite [24] is typically used to calculate the classical neutron rate. However, it requires significant computations and runs on the order of hours which is far from real-time usable. Work has been done to increase the speed by making the simplified realtime RABBIT code [25], but with a timing on the order of 10 s of ms per time step RABBIT requires further performance optimizations to be desirable for the purposes of a real-time controller. Machine learning models provide the opportunity to further speed up this calculation to speeds relevant to realtime control. Previous experiments have begun exploring ways to actively control AEs in real-time. These experiments have shown some control of AEs by calculating an AE amplitude using real-time ECE data and feedback on NBI power [26]. As seen in the the previous experiment’s reference shot 172183, AE’s here are present from about 300 ms to about 1400 ms giving a time range to perform AE control. While the detector model is able to predict different types of AEs, previous experiments lead to focusing control efforts on the reversed shear AEs (RSAEs) that appear strongest in this reference shot.

The rest of the paper is structured as follows: section 2 presents the machine learning models used for AE detection and classical neutron rate calculation, section 3 describes the plasma control system (PCS) real-time implementation of these models and the controller set up, and section 4 discusses experimental results.

## 2. Machine learning models

Recurrent NN excel for temporal analysis of signals [27]. The Reservoir Computing Network (RCN) is composed of 3 computational components: (1) randomized input layer, (2) a reservoir of randomized non-linear neurons fed by delayed input of the reservoir outputs, and (3) the ‘readout’ layer of trained linear neurons driven by the reservoir output. A visualization for the RCN is given in figure 1. The intuition for this method is that the randomly initialized reservoir projects the input feature space to an untrained but typically much larger non-linear feature space in which the data samples can often be more accurately separated. While the RCN architecture is significantly less complex than current state-of-the-art deep learning models, RCNs have shown comparable performance for complex classification and plasma profile prediction tasks [28, 29]. Their simple structure provides additional benefits in both implementation and time to deploy models that will be touched on later in section 3.

2.1. AE classification model

We get the AE amplitude by implementing the AE classification model that was developed in [17]. More details about the training and specifics of this model can be found in [17], but in this work only the key points of the model are summarized. The model utilizes the new real-time accessible, high frequency 40-channel ECE diagnostic that runs at 1 MHz cycle rate. The model works to classify 5 types of AEs: Beta-induced AE, Ellipicity-induced AEs, low-frequency modes, RSAEs, and TAEs. The AE database was hand-labeled by experts and has 450 training and 150 validation discharges; however it is heavily skewed towards RSAE and TAE activity, providing an additional reason to focus control efforts on these two modes. Based on performance metrics and implementation constraints, the model architecture chosen uses a two-layer RCN model with reservoir sizes of 8000 and 500 neurons, respectively. No threshold is assigned as this raw prediction will be used as the reference for the controller, or in other words the control target will be a specific threshold value. For reference, at a threshold of 0.2 this model has a true positive rate (TPR) of 0.93% and 0.97% for RSAEs and TAEs, respectively, and a false positive rate (FPR) of 10% and 19% for RSAEs and TAEs, respectively.

This approach incorporates beam voltage as an input parameter and adopts a RCN architecture to enhance the robustness of the model. The inclusion of beam voltage as an input parameter stems from the intention to use the variable energy and perveance (VEP) algorithm [32, 33] to modulate beam voltage during control. The inclusion of variable beam voltage in order to control AEs is substantiated by experiments where variable beam voltage and perveance altered the stability of various AEs [34, 35]. The transition to the RCN architecture from the single-layer multilayer perceptron model employed in previous works [30, 31] is rooted in the pursuit of enhanced performance through the integration of recurrent connections. Notably, despite the neutron rate calculation lacking temporal dependencies, the incorporation of recurrent connections introduces temporal information from previous inputs. The rationale behind this inclusion of memory is to reduce the impact of noisy inputs by allowing the model to remember previous inputs. This

improves the model’s real-time performance by increasing its resilience to suboptimal inputs, such as noisy electron density or temperature fits, while still delivering accurate neutron rate predictions. ## 3. PCS implementation and controller set-up

3.1. RCN implementation

We have successfully implemented the RCN architecture along with the AE amplitude and neutron rate controllers, which has been integrated into the DIII-D PCS under the RCN algorithm. The comprehensive algorithm oversees various tasks including input acquisition, data pre-processing, model and controller execution, and subsequent output postprocessing. Altogether, these algorithm consistently operate within a cycle time of 1.1 ms and is able to successfully exit if a fault arises due to errors from another algorithm. Additional timing information is seen in figure 3 and when we account for data preprocessing that happens when any model runs, it takes approximately 70µs to preprocess the ECE and plasma state data, 350µs for the NUBEAM RCN to run, and 580µs for the AE amplitude model to run. To achieve such rapid cycle times, an efficient sparse matrix multiplication algorithm has been incorporated, which leverages the inherent sparsity of RCN matrices. Moreover, RCN weights have been directly loaded into the PCS from text files,

*Figure 3. Timing information for different combinations of RCN models turned off and on. This data comes from DIII-D shots 195101 and 195140. There is a break at 1000 ms where different models were switched off and on.*

enhancing the speed of model iteration and testing. In contrast to other machine learning algorithms implemented on the PCS, which require a time-intensive full code review process to modify model weights, typically taking 1–2 weeks, the method of loading weights directly into the PCS GUI allows for swift model deployment between experimental run days. This iterative process greatly expedited the testing of the ML models, rendering this framework highly advantageous and recommendable for future projects seeking rapid iteration capabilities.

3.2. Controller design and implementation

The feedback control strategy has been devised, employing the NBI power as the principal actuator, with the individual beam powers set through the VEP Algorithm [32]. This configuration enables the adjustment of beam voltage and perveance, facilitating a smoother control over the beams [32]. Three controllers have been designed, each predicated on the outputs of the NN model. These controllers, namely the AE amplitude controller, neutron deficit controller, and neutron ratio controller, are standard Proportional-Controllers (P-controllers). The change in NBI power is determined by multiplying the error (error = target-reference) by some constant (Kp) and putting it together gives: ∆PNBI = Kp · error. In the context of the AE amplitude controller, the error term uses the AE amplitude output as reference and a user defined target amplitude on the interval [0,1] as described in figure 4. In the case of the neutron ratio controller, the error term defines the reference sa the ratio between the NN-predicted neutron rate and the real-time neutron measurement while the target is a user-input value as seen in the control schema in figure 5. In a similar vein, the neutron deficit controller takes the reference signal as the difference of the measured neutron rate and the NN-predicted classical neutron rate with a userdefined target deficit value. During experiment, Kp was tuned to optimize the feedback control and account for delays in the system.

3.3. Advanced NBI control

For NBI power modulation, the main controller used is VEP [32]. Although this algorithm has more advanced control capabilities, here it is used for total beam power modulation. The decision to implement this beam control algorithm over the standard one was made because VEP has the option to modulate beam perveance and voltage, resulting in smoother power control.

Neutral beam injection works by accelerating ions with an accelerator voltage, Vacc, coming from the accelerator source at current Iacc. In normal NBI control, perveance is chosen (p =

Iacc/V3/2 acc ) to minimize beam divergence [36]. This optimal perveance value changes as beam voltage changes so perveance is typically normalized to this optimal value at a given voltage. In normal NBI control, perveance tracks voltage to stay at the optimal normalized value of 1, but in this advanced

NBI control perveance will adjust slightly around that optimal value to get fast feedback control and additional NBI power. The total power is then calculated with Pinj = IaccVacc, neglecting the many loss terms. Typically, the NBI power control is done with just duty cycle control, holding voltage fixed and perveance at the optimal value. Duty cycle modulation entails alternating the accelerator beam voltage on and off very rapidly. However, NBI duty cycle modulation is limited because the beams will have a minimum on and a minimum off time, typically 5 ms and 9 ms, respectively. This means that the beam power is not a continuous range from e.g. 0 to 2.5 MW, but instead has the options of 0 MW; a range from 0.5 to 2 MW; and 2.5 MW. This is especially problematic in high and low power experiments where fine beam power modulation is desirable and the gaps from 0 to 0.5 MW and 2 to 2.5 MW are desirable operation regimes for the beams. This is a problem for the traditional beam controller too and is typically dealt with by fixing some NBI at duty cycles of 1 or 0 at the cost of limiting the control space of possible NBI powers. Together with duty cycle modulation, finer NBI control is achieved by also incorporating variable voltage and perveance to the set of actuators. The beam optimizer adjusts all actuators: duty cycle, perveance, and voltage, at every step to make

the control as smooth as possible and avoid hitting the constraints on any of the actuators. Variable voltage is also thought to be useful for AE control [34] as it changes the EP distribution. Beam voltage affects the speed at which the ions are injected into the plasma while perveance changes the density, both of which change the resulting bumps on the EP distribution caused by NBIs. Typical limits for variable voltage ranges are ±5 kV from the initial voltage with a maximum of 80 kV for all except the 150 left beamline which runs at a slightly higher voltage for diagnostic purposes. For variable perveance, shots are typically operated within ±5% of the reference perveance value, which changes depending on the exact beam voltage. This is not necessarily a hard limit on perveance, but the further from the ideal perveance value the greater the likelihood of a beam dropping out mid-shot. Figure 6 shows a shot where VEP was used to test out the feed-forward programmed variable voltage and variable perveance tracking on the 330 right beam. The voltage properly follows the programmed path from 75 kV up to 80 kV, then down to 70 kV before increasing again in figure 6(b). Note there is a delay of about 100 ms between the requested and real voltage as seen in figure 6(b) which was later found out to be caused by a piece of hardware. During this time, the perveance

## 4. Experimental results

In this section, model predictions from experiment are presented and analyzed as well as the controllers being deployed in experiment. While limited control results make full detailed comparisons difficult, it is worth noting that the two different control schema have different scenario goals and cannot be accurately compared. The ECE-based AE amplitude model works well at predicting AEs in the fast ramp-up portion of the shot where unreliable and rapidly changing real-time EFIT data makes the NUBEAMRCN model less reliable. Whereas in a high qmin type scenario that has much higher toroidal magnetic field, the larger field shifts the ECE locations to where the ECE-based model can no longer predict AEs. This more stable flattop is also better for the neutron control schema since the real-time EFITs are more stable compared to the ramp-up portion of the shot.

4.1. Model prediction results

The prediction models were executed in two shot configurations: the high qmin scenario [19, 20] and a standard inner wall limited plasma, both of which exhibit vulnerability to AEs. In the context of the high qmin scenario, it is well-documented that AEs manifest during steady-state operations, exerting substantial detrimental impact on confinement. The performance of the neutron rate predictor in a high qmin scenario shot is depicted in figure 7(a). The shot had less NBI power than is optimal for a high qmin scenario and thus has a reduced presence of AEs as seen in the CO2 interferometer spectra in figure 7(b). Without the presence of AEs, the deficit between the classical neutron rate prediction and the actual measured neutron rate is negligible, but it is clear the predicted neutron rate is reasonable. There is a gap where the neutron rate model greatly overpredicts the rate from 4 to 5 s. This inaccuracy is caused by an NBI dropping out and the model was predicting a neutron rate based off of a larger NBI power than was actually delivered to the plasma. Even with this failure of inputs to the model, the result is not wildly inaccurate and remains relatively stable. Shifting focus to figure 7(c), the performance of the AE amplitude model in the context of the inner wall limited plasma is observed. In this scenario, a pronounced occurrence of AEs is anticipated during the shot’s ramp-up phase spanning from the commencement to approximately 1.5 s. These AEs are seen in the CO2 interferometer spectra in figure 7(d). This model adeptly captures the sharp spikes indicative of RSAEs and TAEs around this time interval. Furthermore, the shot under consideration also exhibits an additional RSAE and TAE spike close to 2 s, which is also present in the CO2 spectra, which coincides with a significant surge in NBI power

that excites these modes. Subsequent to this, a decline in the amplitude of the TAEs is observed toward the end of the shot duration. Statistical results for the models in the DIII-D PCS are shown in figure 8. For the experimental results of the AE amplitude model in figure 8(a), 17 shots were hand-labeled shots by looking at CO2 cross-power spectrograms to look for RSAEs as they were the most prevalent and useful for control. These 17 shots produced 17 412 time slices to calculate the TPR and FPR used in the ROC curve. The model performed with an area under the ROC curve of 0.968 and performs with a 90% TPR at an 8% FPR which is on par with the offline performance of the AE amplitude model. It is worth noting that as with the training data, the handmade labels introduce uncertainties into the model evaluation. For the neutron rate model in figure 8(b), 24 shots were analyzed to give 5241 time slices. This data produces an R2 of 0.768 which is slightly lower than seen in training. This drop in performance can be attributed to two main factors: out of distribution prediction and the sim-to-real gap. For the former, we clearly see points at large NUBEAM neutron rate values above 4 × 1015 which were not present in the training dataset as well as significant number of points at extremely low NUBEAM neutron rates close to 0. Training shots with very low neutron rates were predominantly ignored as that meant shots without NBI power and was not expected to be relevant for the control experiments. Expanding the training dataset to include more training data covering these parameter spaces should alleviate this problem going forward. The sim-to-real gap is a performance hit caused by the difficulty in matching offline training data to the real-time diagnostic data received in the PCS. These problems mainly stem from challenges in reproducing the realtime equilibria and profiles in historic shots. Improving older PCS data providing algorithms to record data offline better to provide more accurate offline data will help close this sim-toreal gap. Based on the model performance, control efforts were predominantly focused towards the AE amplitude control presented in the next section as the AE amplitude model performed better in the PCS compared to the NUBEAMRCN model. The NUBEAMRCN control was also tested but faced DIII-D technical difficulties that limited performance. The NUBEAMRCN control results are presented in the final part of this section.

Upon reaching the 800 ms, the target amplitude increases to 0.8 where the NBI power noticeably drops. With the NBI power at its maximum, the RSAE amplitude is unable to rise back up to the target and eventually continues to drop.

4.3. Neutron rate control

The neutron rate feedback controller was also tested in experiment, although experimental limitations and significant technical challenges prevented optimal testing of the controller. figure 10 overviews the controller’s performance during experiment. In figure 10(a) the neutron model’s classical neutron

rate prediction is compared to the measured neutron rate. In this shot, the required 6 co-orientation beams for a high qmin scenario were not available, so there are no AEs present and the two agree well. This is apparent in figure 10(b) where the ratio of measured over classical neutron rate is plotted and stays around unity. Since this plasma was in a ‘safe’ region where there are no AEs, the controller wants to increase power in an effort to decrease the ratio of measured to classical neutrons. In figure 10(c), the requested power increases since the neutron ratio target does not decrease until one of the NBI drops out around 4500 ms followed by another around 5000 ms. The more interesting feedback control going on is happening with the NBI on the 330 right beamline. In figure 10(d) the requested power is plotted and is far below the power received since there are not enough other beams capable of providing the requested power. The 330 right beamline is set to duty cycle of 1, so all the changes in power are coming from real-time feedback changes to the beam voltage and perveance. In figure 10(e) the beam voltage increases over time to attempt to increase total power from that beamline. It follows a fixed ramp rate until 4200 ms where it is at 75 kV and then the requested beam voltage jumps to the maximum of 79 kV. Beam voltage is a slow actuator and can move at a maximum of 10 kV s−1, so it takes around 400 ms for the beam

Perveance is supposed to be a fast actuator and change quickly, so the requested perveance rises rapidly to be 1.05, the maximum of the allowable perveance range. Further refinements to the experimental set-up and future experimental time would provide the opportunity to further test this feedback controller.

## 5. Conclusion

The real-time integration of the RCN models yielded considerable success, culminating in the accurate predictions of the neutron rate and AE amplitudes in real-time. The implemented controller exhibited success in following to RSAE amplitude targets, operating within the constraints imposed by NBI programming. It is important to note, however, that a notable delay exists between the initiation of controller actions and the ensuing response of the AE amplitude model. A future controller that accounts for this inherent delay would likely represent a significant advance. In experiment, the NBI power as an actuator was found to have limitations in fully controlling AE amplitudes. Voltage control will be enhanced in the future as the data from these experiments is incorporated into the training database. One caveat for data-driven models performing variable voltage control is this data is very rare in the DIII-D shot database. This poses a unique opportunity for a data-driven model that combine information from experiment and physics simulation that model the effects of variable voltage. Furthermore, the incorporation of alternate actuators, such as electron cyclotron heating or plasma shape parameters,

In summary, this work effectively demonstrates the utility of machine learning in AE control while giving an update on the current state of AE controllers implemented on DIII- D. This achievement paves the way for forthcoming enhancements, as the field stands poised to capitalize on future refinements that will invariably bolster machine-learning-based control strategies.
